STEPHANE DE SAKUTIN/Getty images The bird flu outbreak that has killed nearly 185 million birds raised for food since 2022 is still spreading this summer, with fresh detections confirmed by the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service in commercial poultry flocks across 12 states in its latest June 2026 update. The wave — spanning laying hen operations, broiler chicken facilities, and turkey farms concentrated in the Midwest and South — arrives just as egg prices had finally fallen back to near-normal levels after a brutal 2025 peak. Those prices could rise again. And the reason this outbreak is still happening, four years in, points directly to a federal policy decision that licensed experts call unsustainable: the refusal to vaccinate. What the June 2026 Detections Mean for Your Grocery Bill The egg price story of 2026 is best told as a market that swung violently and is not yet stable. After retail egg prices peaked at $6.23 per dozen on average in March 2025, aggressive flock rebuilding and reduced outbreak pressure sent prices plunging. The USDA Economic Research Service reported the average retail price of a dozen eggs at $2.19 in May 2026, down 35.2% from the same month in 2025. At wholesale, prices hit extreme lows — some grades trading below a dollar per dozen in early 2026 as the market swung into oversupply. The oversupply has a structural floor, however. Each new HPAI flock detection triggers mandatory depopulation of all birds on the affected premises, and the losses accumulate quickly. U.S. egg producers destroyed approximately 12.4 million commercial laying hens in 2026 through the spring, compared to just 5.4 million in the entire second half of 2025, according to WATT Poultry . The USDA ERS documents that large-scale flock depopulations typically translate into retail egg price increases within six to eight weeks of outbreak events. With multiple June detections now confirmed, renewed upward pressure on egg prices heading into late summer is plausible — even as the USDA's full-year 2026 forecast still projects an overall 30.4% price decline compared to 2025. Broiler chicken prices rose 1.3% from April to May 2026 and are predicted to increase 1.6% for the full year, according to the USDA ERS June 2026 Food Price Outlook. Read more: Funds Flying the Coop: $100M Budget Allocated to Protect Cows from US Bird Flu Spread Why Bird Flu Keeps Coming Back: The Policy Gap Behind the Price Gap The sustained outbreak is not simply bad luck. It is, according to a growing number of veterinary scientists, the predictable outcome of a federal policy that has never changed: mandatory flock depopulation without vaccination. Ellen P. Carlin and Gwendolen Reyes-Illg, senior policy adviser and president, respectively, of the Veterinary Association for Farm Animal Welfare, published a direct challenge to USDA policy in January 2026. The U.S. strategy, they wrote, has created a "Groundhog Day" cycle — a winter explosion of bird flu, mass animal destruction, barn restocking, then repeat. Their analysis of USDA data showed almost no ground gained since the beginning of the outbreak in 2022, with January 2025 marking the single worst month on record. The solution they describe is already licensed and proven: France adopted poultry vaccination in 2023 and saw outbreaks drop by 96% over two years. USDA has paid to develop effective H5N1 vaccines but has not deployed them, citing trade risks — poultry vaccination can complicate exports if trading partners require vaccination-free status. That calculation has cost consumers an estimated $14.5 billion in higher egg costs in a single outbreak year, plus more than $1.8 billion in taxpayer-funded indemnification payments to farmers in the first three years of the outbreak alone. The USDA's five-pronged $1 billion strategy, announced in February 2025, does include $100 million for vaccine research and development aimed at reducing depopulation. As of mid-2026, no vaccination program for commercial poultry has been deployed. How Bird Flu Stays One Step Ahead: The Science of Clade 2.3.4.4b Understanding why this outbreak has defied four years of federal response requires looking at the virus itself. The strain driving current detections, designated clade 2.3.4.4b, carries three synergistic molecular adaptations that make it unusually dangerous compared to older H5N1 variants. First, dual substitutions in the hemagglutinin protein (G226L and N224K) broaden the virus's receptor-binding range, giving it enhanced potential to attach to human cell receptors. Second, the virus retains a long-stalk neuraminidase structure from recombination with North American wild bird strains, improving its mobility through mammalian respiratory mucus — a structural feature that helps it spread between cattle and other mammals. Third, the PB2-E627K mutation, identified in both animal and some human samples, is associated with more efficient viral replication in mammalian host cells. The critical escalation is that clade 2.3.4.4b is now endemic in wild birds globally — a status the strain had not achieved before 2020. Endemic wild-bird circulation means the virus can be continuously reintroduced to poultry farms through contact with migratory waterfowl, contaminated equipment, and farm workers, regardless of how many commercial flocks are depopulated. Dr. Ed Hutchinson, professor of molecular and cellular virology at the University of Glasgow, described the situation plainly: the virus is "completely out of control" as a disease of wild animals, with no feasible containment method beyond watching it infect vast animal populations. That endemic wild-bird status is precisely why stamping-out cannot achieve eradication. Depopulation eliminates infected flocks; it cannot eliminate the reservoir that continuously reseeds them. Who Has Actually Been Infected: H5N1 Outbreak Risk by the Numbers As of early 2026, 71 Americans had been infected with H5N1 during the current outbreak cycle, resulting in two deaths. The vast majority involved direct occupational exposure — farm workers and dairy employees in prolonged contact with infected animals. Globally, more than 1,000 sporadic human H5N1 infections have been recorded since 1997, with approximately 48% proving fatal — though older, more lethal H5N1 clades from Southeast Asia drive most of that historical mortality rate. Dr. Jeremy Rossman, honorary senior lecturer in virology at the University of Kent, has emphasized that high levels of viral circulation across multiple species increase the statistical likelihood that the virus will acquire the mutations needed to spread efficiently between people. Extensive surveillance of animal populations and rapid identification of human spillover cases, he has written, are what allow for early detection of new mutations that could affect transmissibility. That surveillance remains uneven in the United States. Most confirmed U.S. human cases involved farm workers with known animal exposure who were actively monitored; cases detected through routine flu surveillance systems — people not previously identified as having animal contact — remain a small fraction of the total. The CDC's current risk assessment: low for the general public. Higher-risk individuals include farm and dairy workers with direct animal contact, veterinarians and responders working outbreak sites, and anyone handling raw or unpasteurized dairy products. Is Your Food Safe? What the Evidence Actually Says Yes — with one practical qualifier. H5N1 does not survive proper cooking. Poultry cooked to an internal temperature of 165°F eliminates any H5N1 risk. Eggs with fully set yolks are safe. Pasteurized eggs and egg products pose no risk. The FDA has confirmed through retail sampling that commercial pasteurized dairy products show no viable H5N1 virus. There are no documented cases of H5N1 contracted from properly cooked food. Raw egg preparations carry additional caution during active outbreaks. Hollandaise sauce, soft-poached eggs, runny omelets, and Caesar dressing made with uninspected farm-fresh eggs warrant extra care until outbreak conditions stabilize. Commercial eggs from USDA-inspected facilities continue to meet standard safety requirements and are subject to ongoing USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service testing. Raw or unpasteurized milk is a separate concern entirely. During active outbreaks affecting dairy cattle, raw milk from infected herds can carry live H5N1 virus and should be avoided. What Virologists Want From Here Scientists are not sounding a fire alarm — but the concern level among experts is higher than at any point in the current outbreak's history. The combination of an endemic wild-bird reservoir, more than 1,000 dairy herds infected across 17 states since March 2024, documented mammalian adaptations in clade 2.3.4.4b, and inconsistent surveillance of farm workers creates conditions that virologists watch with sustained attention. Antivirals including oseltamivir (Tamiflu) remain effective against current clade 2.3.4.4b strains when given early. Pre-pandemic H5N1 vaccine candidates exist for human use. COVID-era diagnostic infrastructure would accelerate pandemic response if needed. According to the Contagion Live analysis published this week, the costs associated with the ongoing outbreak since November 2024 have exceeded $1.4 billion, including $1.25 billion in indemnity and compensation payments alone. The USDA's $100 million Poultry Innovation Grand Challenge, announced in April, is now accepting proposals for diagnostics, biosecurity, surveillance, and vaccine candidates. Whether those investments translate into a policy change before the next outbreak cycle is the central unresolved question. Hutchinson's message to readers of BBC Science Focus captured the expert consensus well: there are reasons for both hope and alarm — but no reason to be relaxed. Frequently Asked Questions Can I get bird flu from eating eggs or chicken at a restaurant or grocery store? No. The virus is killed by heat. Poultry cooked to 165°F and eggs with fully set yolks are safe. There are no documented cases of H5N1 contracted from properly cooked food, and commercial eggs from USDA-inspected facilities undergo ongoing safety testing. Will egg prices go back up because of the June 2026 bird flu detections? Possibly in the near term. After falling from the March 2025 peak of $6.23 per dozen, the retail average reached $2.19 in May 2026. New flock losses from June detections could push prices modestly higher within six to eight weeks. The USDA's full-year 2026 projection still shows an overall price decline of 30.4% compared to 2025, but localized supply disruptions could produce short-term spikes. Why does bird flu keep returning every year despite the federal response? Because the response strategy eliminates infected flocks rather than vaccinating them, and the virus is now permanently established in wild bird populations that continuously reintroduce it to farms. Named veterinary scientists — including the president of the Veterinary Association for Farm Animal Welfare — have called the depopulation-only approach unsustainable. France, which adopted poultry vaccination in 2023, saw outbreaks drop by 96%. The United States has licensed vaccines but has not deployed them, citing potential disruptions to poultry export markets. Is bird flu close to becoming a human pandemic? Not imminently, according to current scientific consensus. No sustained human-to-human H5N1 transmission has been confirmed anywhere. Virologists note, however, that clade 2.3.4.4b carries three specific molecular adaptations that enhance its ability to infect mammalian cells, and the scale of animal infections — nearly 185 million birds raised for food lost since 2022, plus more than 1,000 dairy herds — creates additional opportunities for the virus to mutate with each new spillover event. ⓒ 2026 TECHTIMES.com All rights reserved.
